YEAR 11 · UNIT 1 · Computer systems

Numbers and characters in a computer

Follow the allocated lessons for this chapter

Binary, decimal and hexadecimal are different ways to write a number. Character encodings connect numbers with text.

Follow this lesson: reading → example → activity → feedback → revision

Unit 1 representation; later CPU/performance activity is supporting context. Use 8-bit unsigned values and the place weights 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Read the hexadecimal worked section before the mixed conversions.

  1. Read: Place value changes with the base.
  2. Study the worked example: Hexadecimal is a compact notation. Predict one step before reading its result.
  3. Try activity 01: Represent an unsigned value. Reproduce the worked conversion of 45, then independently convert 58 and 10100110 and test the declared 8-bit boundaries. Show place-value working.
  4. Keep your first attempt, then check the matching explained answers. Compare both numeric value and stated width with the Activity 01 key. If hexadecimal digits are reversed, label both nibbles before converting again.
  5. Retrieve this topic without notes. Use the chapter question first; wider syllabus checklists can include later learning. Do not tick a requirement until you can explain it independently.

After feedback, try a changed case: Close the key. Convert 75 to 8-bit binary and hexadecimal, then check it by summing place values: 01001011 and 4B. Cover these expected results until you have attempted it. Next lesson choose a new value and explain the 255/256 boundary.

More practice when ready: Separate characters from encoded bytes · Explain processing and a performance bottleneck.

YEAR 11 · UNIT 1 · Programming and design

Repeating work with loops

Follow the allocated lessons for this chapter

A loop repeats instructions. This repetition is called iteration. Decide what repeats, what changes, and what makes the loop stop.

Follow this lesson: reading → example → activity → feedback → revision

Unit 1 programming practice. Read variables, integer arithmetic and selection first. Trace the accumulator before changing the loop.

  1. Read: A fixed number of repetitions.
  2. Study the worked example: Trace the running total. Predict one step before reading its result.
  3. Try activity 01: Count and accumulate. Predict the supplied three-round example. Then complete A and B independently, recording expected results before running Python or doing a labelled hand trace.
  4. Keep your first attempt, then check the matching explained answers. Compare A, B and the exit with the explained key. If only the last value survives, check that initialisation is outside the loop; if n = 1 gives zero, check the excluded range stop.
  5. Retrieve this topic without notes. Use the chapter question first; wider syllabus checklists can include later learning. Do not tick a requirement until you can explain it independently.

After feedback, try a changed case: Close the key. Use n = 3: predict 6, trace every update and explain why the loop includes 3. Return next lesson with n = 5; predict before running.

YEAR 11 · UNIT 1 · Networks

Network foundations

Follow the allocated lessons for this chapter

When you open a website, several network jobs happen together. Follow the message and learn which layer handles each job.

Follow this lesson: reading → example → activity → feedback → revision

Unit 1 network reasoning. Know the difference between a local link and another network. Use the simplified devices and roles in the worked path; no packet capture or specialist pod is needed.

  1. Read: Four layers, four responsibilities.
  2. Study the worked example: Protocols in a familiar journey. Predict one step before reading its result.
  3. Try activity 01: Follow a message. Draw the simplified remote-server path, then try the local-switch case and the cached-page diagnosis. Name the evidence you would request before selecting a fault.
  4. Keep your first attempt, then check the matching explained answers. Use the Activity 01 key to compare each forwarding responsibility. If every box is a router, relabel access, local forwarding and routing before retrying.
  5. Retrieve this topic without notes. Use the chapter question first; wider syllabus checklists can include later learning. Do not tick a requirement until you can explain it independently.

After feedback, try a changed case: Close the key. Change the destination to a different subnet: explain why the router is now required. Next lesson explain why a cached page alone cannot establish that DNS works.

More practice when ready: Compare transport using a supplied trace.

YEAR 11 · UNIT 2 · Databases and SQL

Getting started with SQL

Follow the allocated lessons for this chapter

Ask the equipment-loan database a question using SQL. You will choose columns, filter rows and sort the result, then compare it with the source records.

Follow this lesson: reading → example → activity → feedback → revision

Unit 2 beginner SQL; grouped reports come later. Complete activity 01 on keys and the supplied Member/Loan tables before activity 02. Practice SELECT and ORDER BY before filters, joins or groups.

  1. Read: Choose result columns with SELECT.
  2. Study the worked example: Make order and duplicates deliberate. Predict one step before reading its result.
  3. Try activity 02: Select and order records. Use this pack’s Member/Loan dataset, not the chapter’s different database. Open files/practice.sqlite OR run files/setup.sql once in a fresh SQLite database. Keep the Activity 01 tables beside you for paper practice.
  4. Keep your first attempt, then check the matching explained answers. Compare column order, every row and the secondary sort with the Activity 02 key. A correct-looking first row is insufficient. SELECT reads rows; it does not change stored data.
  5. Retrieve this topic without notes. Use the chapter question first; wider syllabus checklists can include later learning. Do not tick a requirement until you can explain it independently.

After feedback, try a changed case: Close the key. Return item and loan_id from Loan, ordered by item ascending then loan_id descending. Camera rows should be 103 then 101. Next lesson change the secondary order and explain which rows move.

More practice when ready: Filter rows and test boundaries.
